title: Y in Haskell
description: Haskell's lazy evaluation runs the original Y combinator directly. The page shows the type and definition, why the standard term fails to type-check, and how fix from Data.Function does the job.

steps.description: This is the Haskell version of the Y combinator. The page says Haskell is lazy, so the original Y works directly without eta-expansion, and the comment on line 3 states that. `y :: (a -> a) -> a` is the type, and `y f = let x = f x in x` is the definition. The comment gives the equivalent form `y f = f (y f)`.
`import Data.Function (fix)` brings in Haskell's fixed-point function. `y` takes a function `f` and returns a value of the same type, using `let x = f x in x`.
The comments explain why Haskell's type system rejects the standard lambda-calculus Y: it would require an infinite type, `α = α -> α`. The comment says to use `fix` from `Data.Function` instead.
`factorial` is written with `fix`. It takes a recursive-call stub `rec` and a number `n`, returns 1 when `n` is 0, and otherwise multiplies `n` by `rec (n - 1)`.
The last comment gives the definition of `fix`: `fix f = f (fix f)`. It notes that Haskell's laziness makes it work.

steps.question: The page says the Y combinator finds the fixed point for any generator. What is a fixed point?
steps.answer: a value that a function maps to itself
